evidence.statement: FDA prescribing information for Tasigna (nilotinib), October 2007: a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for chronic myeloid leukemia; boxed warning for QT prolongation and sudden deaths; ten warnings and precautions from myelosuppression to pregnancy.

relevance.statement: Nilotinib is an approved inhibitor of the ABL1 (BCR-ABL) kinase at clinical doses.
relevance.verbatim_sentence: Tasigna (nilotinib) is a kinase inhibitor indicated for the treatment of chronic phase and accelerated phase Philadelphia chromosome positive chronic myelogenous leukemia.

relevance.statement: The label carries a boxed warning for QT prolongation and sudden deaths.
relevance.verbatim_sentence: WARNING: QT PROLONGATION AND SUDDEN DEATHS.

safety.boxed_reason: Tasigna prolongs the QT interval; sudden deaths have been reported in patients receiving nilotinib
safety.boxed_text: WARNING: QT PROLONGATION AND SUDDEN DEATHS. Tasigna prolongs the QT interval. Sudden deaths have been reported in patients receiving nilotinib. Tasigna should not be used in patients with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, or long QT syndrome. Hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia must be corrected prior to Tasigna administration and should be periodically monitored. Drugs known to prolong the QT interval and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. Patients should avoid food 2 hours before and 1 hour after taking dose. Use with caution in patients with hepatic impairment. ECGs should be obtained to monitor the QTc at baseline, seven days after initiation, and periodically thereafter, as well as following any dose adjustments.

sections.heading: Myelosuppression
sections.detail: Associated with neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and anemia; CBC every 2 weeks for the first 2 months, then monthly; reversible by withholding dose

sections.heading: QT prolongation
sections.detail: Tasigna prolongs the QT interval; correct hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia before administration and monitor periodically; ECGs at baseline, seven days after initiation, periodically thereafter and after dose adjustments

sections.heading: Sudden deaths
sections.detail: Sudden deaths reported in the safety population and the expanded access program; ventricular repolarization abnormalities may have contributed

sections.heading: Elevated serum lipase
sections.detail: Caution in patients with a history of pancreatitis; check serum lipase periodically

sections.heading: Liver function abnormality
sections.detail: Elevations in bilirubin, AST/ALT and alkaline phosphatase; check hepatic function tests periodically

sections.heading: Electrolyte abnormalities
sections.detail: Hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia and hyponatremia; correct before initiating and monitor periodically

sections.heading: Hepatic impairment
sections.detail: Not investigated; caution recommended and the QT interval monitored closely

sections.heading: Drug interactions
sections.detail: Avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers; if a strong inhibitor must be co-administered, consider dose reduction and monitor the QT interval closely

sections.heading: Food effects
sections.detail: Food increases blood levels of Tasigna; avoid food 2 hours before and 1 hour after a dose

sections.heading: Pregnancy
sections.detail: Fetal harm can occur when administered to a pregnant woman

safety.contraindications: Do not use in patients with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, or long QT syndrome.
safety.indication: chronic phase and accelerated phase Philadelphia chromosome positive chronic myelogenous leukemia in adults resistant to or intolerant to prior therapy that included imatinib

evidence.statement: Open-label phase 1 of nilotinib in 119 patients with imatinib-resistant CML or Ph+ ALL (Kantarjian 2006, NEJM).

relevance.statement: Nilotinib inhibited BCR-ABL kinase activity and produced hematologic and cytogenetic responses in imatinib-resistant CML.
relevance.verbatim_sentence: Nilotinib is a highly selective inhibitor of Bcr-Abl and has activity in imatinib-resistant CML.

evidence.statement: c-Abl phosphorylates parkin and inhibits its ubiquitin ligase and protective function; increased in postmortem Parkinson's striatum (Ko 2010, PNAS).
evidence.source_name: Ko 2010, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA

relevance.verbatim_sentence: Tyrosine phosphorylation of parkin is increased in the striatum of patients with Parkinson disease.

evidence.statement: c-Abl-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation of parkin in MPTP mice and in Parkinson's substantia nigra (Imam 2011, J Neurosci).

evidence.statement: c-Abl phosphorylates alpha-synuclein at Y39 and regulates its degradation; the phosphorylated form is increased in Parkinson's brain (Mahul-Mellier 2014, Hum Mol Genet).

relevance.statement: c-Abl phosphorylates alpha-synuclein at tyrosine 39, and the phosphorylated form is increased in Parkinson's brain tissue.
relevance.verbatim_sentence: Y39-phosphorylated alpha-synuclein is increased in brains of Parkinson disease patients.

evidence.statement: In alpha-synuclein transgenic mice, nilotinib increased autophagic clearance of alpha-synuclein, reversed dopamine neuron loss and improved motor behaviour (Hebron 2013, Hum Mol Genet).

relevance.statement: In transgenic mice, nilotinib increased autophagic clearance of alpha-synuclein, reversed dopamine neuron loss and improved motor behaviour.

evidence.statement: Nilotinib protected dopaminergic neurons and reduced c-Abl activation in the MPTP mouse model (Karuppagounder 2014, Sci Rep).

relevance.statement: Nilotinib protected dopaminergic neurons and reduced c-Abl activation in the MPTP mouse model.

strongest_case_for.text: Nilotinib is an approved ABL1 (BCR-ABL) kinase inhibitor, so the target engagement it needs is a known pharmacology rather than a hypothesis.
Three independent groups report c-Abl activation and its consequences for parkin and alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's brain tissue, which ties the target to the disease biology.
In two mouse models from two groups, nilotinib cleared alpha-synuclein and protected dopaminergic neurons.
An open-label pilot of 12 patients reported improved motor and cognitive scores and detected nilotinib in cerebrospinal fluid.

strongest_case_against.text: Brain exposure is contested: in leukemia patients the CSF/plasma ratio was 0.53 % (range 0.23–1.5 %), a fraction of a percent, while the pilot only reports that the drug was detectable.
The only human efficacy signal is open-label, in 12 patients, with no placebo arm; every participant knew they were on the drug.
Target engagement in the human brain has never been measured; the mouse biology has not been shown to occur in patients.
Safety is a standing constraint: the label carries a boxed warning for QT prolongation and sudden deaths, and the likely Parkinson's trial population is older and on other QT-prolonging drugs.

2016-07-11.opinion: Based on the evidence visible as of 2016-07-11, Elute would make no clear prioritization of nilotinib for Parkinson's disease: the mechanism and disease relevance are established, but brain exposure is contested, target engagement in patients is unknown, and the only clinical signal is a single uncontrolled pilot.
2016-07-11.what_would_change_my_mind: Reproducible CSF exposure compatible with c-Abl inhibition at a tolerated dose, and a human target-engagement readout; then a blinded, placebo-controlled study of the clinical signal.

2026-09-20.opinion: Based on the evidence visible as of 2026-09-20, Elute would deprioritize nilotinib for Parkinson's disease relative to candidates with stronger controlled human evidence, primarily because brain exposure is contested by three measurements, target engagement in patients is unknown, and the controlled clinical evidence is negative in two trials.
2026-09-20.what_would_change_my_mind: Demonstrated CSF exposure compatible with c-Abl inhibition at a tolerated dose in Parkinson's patients together with a reproducible human target-engagement readout; without those, further clinical testing of this hypothesis would be uninterpretable.
